title: Two things
hook: Kant: the starry heavens above and the moral law within fill the mind with awe

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pascal under the night sky, and the silence of the infinite spaces that frightened him. Your line was the silent spaces. Today a second philosopher looks at the same sky and finds a second thing to set beside it.

Two directions. Up, where the stars are. And in, where a sense of duty says: this must be done. Immanuel Kant spent a whole book on duty and reason, argued step by careful step. Then, in its conclusion, he stops arguing and writes something closer to a confession. Two things, he says, fill the mind with admiration and awe, and the feeling grows the more often and the more steadily we think about them. The starry heavens above. And the moral law within.
screen: `UP, WHERE THE STARS ARE.` → `IN, WHERE DUTY SPEAKS.` → `TWO THINGS.`

segments.voice: First, the pairing. Stars are easy to stand in awe of. Kant sets beside them something that doesn't shine at all: the sense, inside a person, that some things must be done and some must not, whatever they cost. He says he doesn't have to hunt for either one as if it were hidden in darkness. He sees them both in front of him, and ties them straight to the awareness of his own existence. Second, the sky. The view of a countless crowd of worlds, Kant says, seems to wipe out his importance, as a creature of matter who must give that matter back to the planet he stands on. Pascal felt that smallness as fear. Kant names it plainly and doesn't look away. Third, the law within. Here the arithmetic flips. The same person who shrinks under the stars is raised up by the moral law, given a worth that doesn't depend on size, or the body, or the world of things. Fourth, the growing. A view seen every day can wear thin. Kant claims the opposite for these two: the oftener and the more steadily you reflect, the more they fill the mind. Some readers hear in that a practice, not just a feeling: looking up, and looking in, every day, and finding they don't wear out.
screen: `TWO THINGS: ABOVE AND WITHIN` · `THE STARS MAKE A PERSON SMALL` · `THE LAW WITHIN MAKES A PERSON LARGE` · `AWE THAT GROWS WITH LOOKING` · then, large: `ABOVE AND WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Look up first, at the sky through a window or outside, or at whatever is above you, and let it be bigger than you are. Then close your eyes and turn the same attention inward: is there one thing you already know is right to do, a call owed, a truth to tell, a kindness put off? Don't argue with it; just look at it, the way you looked at the sky.
Two things. Kant's pair: the starry heavens above, the moral law within, and the awe that grows the longer you look at them. Today's word.
Your line: above and within. The stars shrink you, and the law within lifts you back up. Day one thousand seventeen, done.

howItsDone: Readers of Kant often meet this passage on its own, and some people who keep a reflective practice pair a look at the night sky with an evening review of their own conduct.
